How to Start a Small Vegetable Garden

A small vegetable garden is one of the easiest ways to eat better and spend more time outside. You do not need a farm or a big yard. A single raised bed, a few pots on a balcony, or a strip of soil along a fence can feed you salad for most of the summer. This guide walks through the first season, step by step, so you can start this weekend.

Pick a sunny spot

Most vegetables need six to eight hours of direct sun each day. Before you buy a single seed, watch your yard for a day and note where the light falls in the morning, at noon and in the late afternoon. A spot that gets sun all afternoon is ideal for tomatoes, peppers and beans. Leafy greens such as lettuce and spinach can cope with a little shade, and they often do better in it when summer gets hot.

Pick a place close to the house if you can. A garden you walk past every day is a garden you will water, weed and pick. A plot at the far end of the yard is easy to forget, and weeds grow fast when nobody is looking. Make sure a hose or a tap is close by too, because carrying water across the yard gets old quickly.

Start with good soil

Good soil does most of the work for you. If you are building a raised bed, fill it with a mix of topsoil and compost, about two parts soil to one part compost. If you are planting straight into the ground, dig out the grass, loosen the soil with a fork, and work in a few inches of compost. Soil that crumbles in your hand when it is damp is just right. Soil that sticks together like clay needs more compost, and soil that runs through your fingers like sand needs it too.

Make your own compost

Compost feeds the plants slowly and helps the soil hold water. You can buy it in bags, or you can make your own from kitchen scraps, leaves and grass clippings. A simple bin in a corner of the yard will turn waste into dark, rich compost in a few months. Add a fresh layer to your beds each spring and the soil will get better every year.

Our soil guide has more on mixing a bed.

Choose easy plants

For a first garden, grow a few plants that are hard to kill and that you like to eat. Lettuce, radishes, beans, zucchini and cherry tomatoes are all good choices. Radishes are ready in about a month, which keeps you interested while the slower plants grow. Herbs such as basil, parsley and chives are easy too, and a handful of fresh herbs makes a plain meal taste much better.

Read the back of each seed packet. It tells you how deep to plant the seed, how far apart to space the plants, and how many days it takes to harvest. Plants that are packed too close together fight for light and water, and they are more likely to get sick. It feels wasteful to thin out tiny seedlings, but the plants that are left will grow bigger and stronger.

Water, mulch and weed

Water deeply and not too often. A good soak two or three times a week is better than a light sprinkle every day, because deep watering pushes roots down where the soil stays cool and damp. Water in the morning if you can, so the leaves dry before night. Push a finger into the soil before you water. If it is dry an inch down, it is time to water. If it is still damp, wait another day.

A layer of mulch, such as straw or shredded leaves, keeps the soil moist and stops most weeds before they start. Spread it around your plants once they are a few inches tall, and leave a small gap around each stem. Pull any weeds you see while they are small. A few minutes of weeding each week is far easier than a long afternoon of it once a month.

See how often to water and growing tomatoes.

Harvest often

Pick your vegetables often. Many plants, such as beans and zucchini, make more food the more you pick. Lettuce tastes best when it is young and tender, and tomatoes are ready when they are fully colored and give a little when you squeeze them. Keep a small notebook of what you planted, when you planted it and how it did. Next spring, that notebook will be the best garden guide you own.
